chapter: Washington clubs, Louis Jordan and Sarah Vaughan, 1949-54
title: Playing the Macombo with Pearl Bailey and losing his band's job
summary: He goes to Hollywood as Pearl's accompanist on promise of better pay, but returns to find his replacement had taken over the club.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: At that particular time, around 1950, the places where people were sent for a showcase were places out in Hollywood, and one of these places was The Macombo in Hollywood. It was a very swank club, and it was... I can remember, when I worked there, that every night it was just packed full of what seemed to be nothing but big movie stars. Anyway, when Pearl got this invitation to come out there, of course, she knew... And I guess her managers and everyone who had set up, they were preparing her for a Hollywood more or less debut, pictures as well as anything else -- and, to make a long story short, for bigger things.

So Pearl came to me and said this would be her big chance. And I had known Pearl since back during the Jelly Roll Morton days in the 30's. And she asked me if I would go out there with her as her accompanist. I made mention of the fact that I would love to go, but first of all, I had my band there, and I couldn't just walk away and leave the band to go on a thing with her. Well, she asked me if she could arrange with the manager of the club for me to put someone in my place until I came back, would it be okay. So now comes the problem with the money -- what kind of money was it? It turned out that the figure I asked for to go out there, she said it was

impossible for her to do it at that particular time. But if I went with her, and she got this big chance, she'd never forget me and she would make it up to me. And this was all in a very persuadin' and almost beggin' situation.

So we got the thing straight with the manager. I put a pianist in my place, and Pearl and I boarded a plane for California. And the results being a very successful... I think it was two or three weeks we were out there. We did the engagement, and we flew back to Washington.

What I found out when I came back, the pianist that I had put in the club, for some reason, had undermined me for the job. He had probably taken it for less money, I would suppose, or something. And when I came back, he had another band, and my band was out in the street. Because while I was gone, I don't know what came up, but he had some other musicians. And when we came back, it was the date that Pearl had chosen to go back into the club.

So when I confronted her with what had happened to my job on account of me going West with her, and what she had said and everything, it seemed to be that it was something that, as she was saying, was understood on quite different terms or something like that. Well, anyway, to finalize that particular scene, Pearl went back in the club, I was without a job and my band was without a job. And this was the kind of

thing that... I've heard Pearl talk a lot about the way she feels about people and certain things, and I often flash back to that, because I never did understand that and she never quite gave me an explanation. And since her climb to fame and everything, words between her and I have been said very sparingly, to like "Hello, how are you?" or something like that.

I was called by Louis Bellson to make a commercial date with her for an automobile company in Washington, and a couple of times when she was on television here I was called on to do some things with her. But the old what was supposed to have been friendship and everything, and closeness, seemed to have disappeared with her career or something like that. I don't know what happened.
